why: Money and big names are piling in. Humanoid robot funding hit a record $8.7B by July, Tesla started Optimus production in Fremont, and Sam Altman says OpenAI's robots will help build data centers.
watch: Whether Tesla's 20,000-a-week ramp stays on schedule, and the first job postings for humanoid service techs.
background: Humanoid robots were lab projects for decades: Honda's ASIMO debuted in 2000 and Boston Dynamics' Atlas in 2013. Cheaper motors and batteries, plus AI that can learn tasks from video, pulled them toward real jobs in the 2020s, and Tesla announced Optimus in 2021.

why: Openings are up 113% since 2022, the fastest of any tracked trade, and new funding keeps putting more robots in the field that need servicing. Training is only starting to catch up, with a new Army role and new college degrees.
watch: More schools adding robotics tech programs is the sign the field is starting to fill up.
background: Factory robots have been common in car plants since the 1980s, but warehouse automation took off after Amazon bought Kiva Systems in 2012, and labor shortages after 2020 pushed more companies to automate. Every robot installed needs people to set it up, program it and fix it.

why: Voters passed 40 of 41 local data center measures on Nov 3-4, and builder stocks fell 17-23% after Texas governor-elect Hinojosa called for a moratorium.
watch: Whether the proposed Texas and NYC pauses become law and cover projects already under construction.
background: Data centers used to be welcomed for their tax revenue. The AI build-out since 2023 made them far bigger, with single campuses using as much power as a small city, which raised local fears about electric bills, water use and generous tax breaks.

why: The AI building boom needs people to keep power and cooling running. Hundreds of thousands of positions are projected unfilled, and only about 15% of applicants qualify.
watch: New training institutes opening in 2027 will add supply. Until then the shortage favors people with electrical and mechanical skills.
background: Data centers need round-the-clock staff to keep power, backup generators and cooling running, because an outage can cost millions an hour. The AI boom since 2023 multiplied construction faster than trade schools could train people.

why: The Fed held at 3.75-4% on Oct 28 in a 10-2 vote with two members wanting a hike, and futures priced about 85% odds of a December hike (market odds, not fact).
watch: The Dec 9 Fed decision and the next inflation report.
background: After inflation hit four-decade highs in 2022, central banks raised rates fast, then cut them in 2024 and 2025 as inflation cooled. Talk of hikes again in 2026 signals inflation has crept back up.

why: Big AI spenders are on pace for roughly $800B in 2026 capex, and the big four are now raising over $131B in debt and equity to pay for it. AMD reported data center revenue up 96.9%.
watch: Whether financing stays easy as Blackstone's Jon Gray warns of debt concentration, or capex guidance gets cut.
background: Big tech has always spent heavily on data centers, but after ChatGPT launched in late 2022 the race to train and run AI models sent spending to records. Investors debate whether revenue will catch up, echoing the fiber-optic overbuild of the late-1990s dot-com boom.

why: Companies are moving agents into real operations: ADNOC is deploying OpenAI Frontier and CrowdStrike launched a kill switch for rogue agents, which creates demand for people who can build and govern them.
watch: More job postings that name agent building or agent security, and whether entry-level roles appear.
background: Early chatbots answered questions; agents take actions on their own, like writing code, booking or filing tickets, using software tools. Frameworks for building them appeared in 2023, and companies started hiring people who can make them reliable in real work.

why: Trading volume on Kalshi and Polymarket jumped about ninefold in seven months, Kalshi sought a $40B valuation, and federal regulators are fighting states over who can limit them.
watch: Court rulings in the regulators-versus-states fight will decide how big this can get.
background: Betting on events was mostly banned or limited in the US. Kalshi won federal approval as a regulated exchange in 2020 and won a court fight to list election contracts in 2024, while Polymarket grew offshore, setting up today's state-versus-federal battle.

why: Weight-loss drugs went mainstream. The Wegovy pill passed 3M US prescriptions in five months, a new oral drug got Medicare coverage at $50 a month, and food giants launched 'GLP-1 friendly' ranges.
watch: Spin-off businesses around it, like food, fitness and clothing, are the next wave.
background: GLP-1 drugs were first approved for type 2 diabetes in 2005. Semaglutide was approved for weight loss as Wegovy in 2021, demand exploded, shortages followed, and pill versions arrived to make them cheaper and easier to take.

why: Gold broke $5,000 an ounce for the first time in January as geopolitical tension sent people to safe havens. It has since cooled, trading roughly $3,900 to $4,200 in October.
watch: Gold tends to move with fear and interest rates: rate hikes usually weigh on it, new conflicts usually lift it.
background: Gold has been a safe haven for thousands of years and tends to rise in crises, from the 1970s inflation to the 2008 financial crisis. Since 2022, central banks, led by China, Poland and Turkey, have bought gold at a record pace to rely less on the US dollar, helping push prices to new highs.

why: Not heating up. The headline '4.8M job gap' hides only about 514K real US postings, and 56% of security professionals say AI is cutting entry-level roles.
watch: Experience, clearances and hands-on skills count for more than certifications alone here.
background: Since the mid-2010s, headlines about millions of unfilled cyber jobs pulled many career-changers and bootcamps into the field. Most openings ask for experience, so entry-level candidates piled up while AI tools started automating basic monitoring work.

why: Viewing is up 18%, to 28.6B minutes in the first half of 2026, and the WNBA is expanding to 18 teams at about $250M per franchise.
watch: New media-rights deals and sponsorships.
background: Interest built for years after the 1999 Women's World Cup, but the big jump came in 2024, when Caitlin Clark's final college season and WNBA debut drew record TV audiences, pushing networks and investors to pay far more for teams and rights.

why: Short vertical soap-opera apps grew installs 238% in Q1, revenue is projected near $14B for 2026, and half of marketers plan their own.
watch: Big studios and streamers launching their own would mark it going mainstream.
background: Micro-dramas, minute-long vertical soap-opera episodes sold by the episode, exploded in China around 2022. Apps like ReelShort and DramaBox brought the format to the US in 2023, though Quibi's 2020 collapse shows short premium video doesn't always work.

why: 24.3M US players in 2025, up 479% since 2020, and the US needs tens of thousands more courts.
watch: Court building versus closures. Padel is already seeing post-boom closures in some countries.
background: Pickleball was invented on Bainbridge Island, Washington, in 1965. It spread slowly through retirement communities until pandemic-era outdoor play made it the fastest-growing US sport, and pro leagues drew celebrity investors.

why: Fading. Pop Mart's online sales fell and its shares dropped about 20% on worries the Labubu craze is cooling.
watch: Resale prices are the earliest tell that a collectible craze is ending.
background: Labubu, an elf-like character by artist Kasing Lung, is sold in blind boxes by Chinese toy maker Pop Mart. It went viral in 2024 after celebrity sightings sent resale prices soaring. Crazes like Beanie Babies in the 1990s show how fast collectibles can cool.

why: Big brewers are pushing it hard, with AB InBev's alcohol-free sales up 27%, but overall growth slowed from 17% to about 9%, a sign it's maturing.
watch: Whether growth keeps slowing. That would mean the market is getting crowded.
background: Alcohol-free beer has existed for over a century, but younger people drinking less, Dry January and better-tasting brews turned it into a growth category in the 2020s, led by brands like Athletic Brewing and Heineken 0.0.

why: Social media demand pushed Kyoto tea prices up about 170%, and Tokyo shops are still rationing tins.
watch: Prices falling as new supply arrives would mean the hype is passing.
background: Matcha is powdered green tea from Japan, traditionally used in tea ceremonies. Social media cafe culture made it a global trend in the 2020s, and supply can't grow quickly because tea plants take years to mature and the shading process is labor-heavy.

why: Fading. Standalone prompt engineer postings are down about 40% from the 2023 peak as the skill folds into other jobs.
watch: This is what a flooded trend looks like. Easy-entry AI jobs can follow the same path.
background: When ChatGPT launched in late 2022, companies briefly posted high-paying prompt engineer jobs. As models got better at understanding plain requests, the skill became something most workers do rather than a job of its own.

why: Courts are still growing about 16% a year worldwide, but Sweden and Chile are already seeing post-boom closures.
watch: Whether the US follows the growth or the closures.
background: Padel was invented in Mexico in 1969 and became huge in Spain and Argentina. It spread across Europe in the late 2010s, and a court-building rush in Sweden turned into a bust around 2022 when too many courts opened.

why: Utilities and equipment makers report huge demand: Dominion counts 54.9GW of data center requests and GE Vernova's backlog hit $197B on gas turbines.
watch: Whether grid operators and regulators slow approvals, or the backlash curbs new projects.
background: Electricity use was flat in the US for about fifteen years because efficiency gains offset growth. Cloud computing and then AI training pushed data center loads up sharply in the 2020s, and utilities began reporting multi-gigawatt interconnection queues.

why: Early whisper: MMI raised $125M for robotic microsurgery, one sighting so far.
watch: A second independent funding or approval signal within 14 days.
background: Robot-assisted surgery began with systems cleared in the 1990s, and Intuitive Surgical's da Vinci became the standard platform in the 2000s. Newer startups aim at finer, microscale procedures.

why: Early whisper: OpenAI says its hardware teams use its models 23x more since February, cutting prototype time to under a month.
watch: A second company reporting AI-sped hardware design within 14 days.
background: Engineers have used software tools to design hardware for decades, from CAD in the 1980s to automated chip layout. Generative AI is the latest layer, aimed at speeding drawings, code and test planning.
